title: C-style strings and <cstring>
relevance: OAs and early SDE rounds still test null-terminated char arrays and the classic <cstring> operations for I/O, copy, search, compare, parse, and tokenize.

phases.goal: Establish what a C-style string is and what <cstring> provides.

must_hit.point: A C-style string is a character array terminated by the null character '\0'.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that the terminator marks where the text ends inside an array that may be larger than the text.

must_hit.point: The <cstring> header is the C++ name for C's string.h and supplies the family of functions for these strings.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names <cstring> / string.h as the library for C-style string operations.

probes: What is a C-style string, and which header do you use for the classic string helpers in C++?

hints.1: Think about how the end of the text is marked inside a char array.
hints.2: Mention the terminator character and the C++ header that wraps string.h.
hints.3: A C-style string is a char array ended by '\0'; <cstring> is C++'s name for string.h.

phases.goal: Check how the core <cstring> operations and related I/O actually behave.

must_hit.point: cin.getline takes the array and its capacity; for char s[100], getline(s, 100) reads up to 99 chars plus '\0' so it does not overrun the buffer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains that passing the size leaves room for the terminating '\0'.

must_hit.point: strcpy(destination, source) copies source character by character, including its '\0', into destination; destination must hold source plus terminator.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes full copy including terminator and the size requirement.

must_hit.point: strncpy(destination, source, length) copies at most length characters, capping how much is written.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts the bounded copy with unbounded strcpy.

must_hit.point: strcat appends source starting at destination's existing '\0' and adds a fresh terminator; strncat appends at most length characters of source.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Can say appending "Morning" onto "Good" yields "GoodMorning", and name the bounded form.

must_hit.point: strstr finds the first substring occurrence and returns a pointer to that match; strchr/strrchr find the first/last occurrence of a character and return a pointer into the string from there.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses an example like strstr("Programming", "gram") returning "gramming", and notes the extra r in strrchr means reverse/last.

must_hit.point: strcmp compares lexicographically by sign: 0 if equal, negative if str1 orders before str2, positive if after; it walks until the first differing character and compares ASCII codes, so case matters ('a' is 97, 'A' is 65).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions sign of return value and that lowercase codes are larger than uppercase, e.g. "apple" vs "banana" is negative because 'a' (97) precedes 'b' (98).

must_hit.point: strtol(str, NULL, base) parses a leading long int in the given base; strtof(str, NULL) parses a float; the middle argument can capture the first unparsed character or be NULL to discard it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls examples like strtol("235", NULL, 10) and strtof("54.78", NULL).

must_hit.point: strtok splits on any delimiter characters: first call passes the string, later calls pass NULL to continue, and NULL is returned when no tokens remain.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the first-call / NULL-continue pattern and that delimiters are the caller's choice.

probes: Walk through strcpy/strncpy, strcat/strncat, the search functions, strcmp's return value, and how strtok is called repeatedly.

hints.1: Group the APIs: copy, append, search, compare, parse, tokenize.
hints.2: For each, say what is written or returned, and call out bounded forms and strtok's NULL continuation.
hints.3: strcpy copies including '\0'; strncpy caps length; strcat/strncat append at the old '\0'; strstr/strchr/strrchr return pointers; strcmp's sign is the result; strtok(str,...) then strtok(NULL,...).

phases.goal: Contrast unbounded vs bounded string writes and first vs last character search.

must_hit.point: strcpy is a full unbounded copy including the terminator, while strncpy lets the caller cap writes to at most length characters.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that strcpy needs a large enough destination, whereas strncpy bounds how much is written.

must_hit.point: strcat appends the whole source (then a terminator), while strncat appends at most length characters of the source.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both forms and the length cap on the bounded append.

must_hit.point: strchr finds the first occurrence of a character; strrchr finds the last (the extra r stands for reverse).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Clearly distinguishes first vs last match and the naming cue.

probes: When would you reach for strncpy/strncat instead of strcpy/strcat, and how do strchr and strrchr differ?

hints.1: Compare the unbounded helpers to their length-capped siblings.
hints.2: Also separate first-occurrence vs last-occurrence character search.
hints.3: strcpy/strcat need enough room and write fully; strncpy/strncat take a length cap; strchr is first, strrchr is last.

phases.goal: Apply getline, conversion, and strtok to concrete input and parsing tasks.

must_hit.point: Read a whole line including spaces into a char array with cin.getline(array, capacity), passing size so the buffer is not overrun.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives a pattern like char s[100]; cin.getline(s, 100); and notes room for '\0'.

must_hit.point: Use strtol/strtof to convert leading numeric text in a C-string into long int or float (e.g. base 10 for strtol).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions converting strings like "235" and "54.78" via those functions.

must_hit.point: With strtok and delimiters "=;", "x=10;y=20;z=35" yields tokens x, 10, y, 20, z, 35; using only ";" yields the key-value chunks "x=10", "y=20", "z=35".
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains that delimiter choice controls whether you get separate keys/values or whole pairs.

probes: How would you read a full name into a char buffer, convert numeric text, and tokenize "x=10;y=20;z=35" as either flat tokens or key-value pairs?

hints.1: Start with getline for spaced input, then parsing/tokenizing.
hints.2: Tie strtol/strtof to numeric strings and strtok's delimiter set to the desired split.
hints.3: getline(s, 100); strtol/strtof for numbers; strtok with "=;" for six tokens or ";" for three key-value pairs.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: strcpy copies the entire source including '\0' and requires a destination large enough for source plus terminator; strncpy copies at most a caller-chosen length, capping how much is written.
strcat appends all of source starting at destination's existing '\0' and adds a fresh terminator; strncat appends at most length characters of source.
strchr returns a pointer to the first occurrence of a character; strrchr returns a pointer to the last (the extra r stands for reverse).

tradeoffs.topic: strtok delimiter set vs key-value layout
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Delimiters "=;" on "x=10;y=20;z=35" produce x, 10, y, 20, z, 35; choosing only ";" yields "x=10", "y=20", "z=35" as key-value pair chunks—the delimiter set is entirely the caller's choice.

gotchas.trap: Calling strcpy without ensuring the destination is large enough.
gotchas.correction: The destination must be large enough to hold the source plus its terminating '\0'.

gotchas.trap: Using cin.getline without passing the buffer capacity.
gotchas.correction: Pass the size so getline stops before overrunning the buffer and leaves room for '\0' (e.g. getline(s, 100) on char s[100] reads up to 99 chars plus '\0').

gotchas.trap: Expecting strcmp to ignore letter case.
gotchas.correction: Comparison uses ASCII codes of the first differing characters; lowercase letters have larger codes than uppercase ('a' is 97, 'A' is 65), so case affects ordering.

gotchas.trap: Passing the original string on every strtok call instead of continuing correctly.
gotchas.correction: The first call passes the string; each later call passes NULL to continue from where the previous one stopped; NULL is returned once no tokens remain.
